et møde.explanation: "Et møde" means "a meeting". To say people hold a meeting, use "at holde" (to hold): "Vi holder et møde i morgen" (We are holding a meeting tomorrow). The verb "at møde" (to meet) is spelled the same. For example, "Jeg møder dig i morgen" (I meet you tomorrow).

sentence.da: Min chef har et **møde** i dag.
sentence.en: My boss has a meeting today.

et mødelokale.explanation: "Et mødelokale" means "a meeting room". It is built from "et møde" (a meeting) and "et lokale" (a room in a building). To talk about a room in a home or a hotel, use "et værelse" (a room): "Jeg sover på mit værelse" (I sleep in my room).

sentence.da: Kollegerne sidder i et **mødelokale** og planlægger det nye projekt.
sentence.en: The colleagues are sitting in a meeting room and planning the new project.

et mønster.explanation: "Et mønster" means "a pattern". To talk about a design on cloth, say: "et mønster med blomster" (a pattern with flowers). To talk about a pattern in what someone does, say: "et mønster i hans opførsel" (a pattern in his behavior).

sentence.da: Der er et fint **mønster** på kjolen.
sentence.en: There is a nice pattern on the dress.

mad.explanation: "Mad" means "food". To say someone cooks, use "at lave mad" (to cook): "Jeg laver mad hver dag" (I cook every day). Do not mix it up with "en mad", which means a sandwich. For example, "en mad med ost" (a sandwich with cheese).

sentence.da: Jeg er sulten og vil have **mad**.
sentence.en: I am hungry and want food.

madlavning.explanation: "Madlavning" means "cooking". It is built from "mad" (food) and "at lave" (to make). To say someone is cooking, use "at lave mad": "Han laver mad" (He is cooking).

sentence.da: Ved **madlavning** bruger vi en gryde og en pande.
sentence.en: When cooking, we use a pot and a pan.

madpapir.explanation: "Et madpapir" means "sandwich paper". It is built from "en mad" (a sandwich) and "et papir" (a paper). The word "papir" also ends "toiletpapir" (toilet paper).

sentence.da: Jeg pakker madderne ind i **madpapir** og lægger dem i tasken.
sentence.en: I wrap the sandwiches in sandwich paper and put them in the bag.

madspild.explanation: "Madspild" means "food waste". It is built from "mad" (food) and "et spild" (waste). To say you want to avoid it, use "at undgå" (to avoid): "Vi vil gerne undgå madspild" (We would like to avoid food waste).

sentence.da: **Madspild** sker, når vi køber mere mad, end vi spiser.
sentence.en: Food waste happens when we buy more food than we eat.

mager.explanation: "Mager" means "lean". To describe a person, it means "skinny": "Han er meget mager" (He is very skinny).

sentence.da: En **mager** bøf har meget lidt fedt.
sentence.en: A lean steak has very little fat.

magi.explanation: "Magi" means "magic". To say a moment feels special, say: "Der er magi i luften" (There is magic in the air).

sentence.da: I eventyret bruger heksen **magi** til at forvandle prinsen til en frø.
sentence.en: In the fairy tale the witch uses magic to turn the prince into a frog.

magisk.explanation: "Magisk" means "magical". It is the adjective for "magi" (magic). To say a moment was wonderful, say: "Det var magisk!" (It was magical!)

sentence.da: Troldmanden har en **magisk** stav i hånden.
sentence.en: The wizard has a magic wand in his hand.

magtfuld.explanation: "Magtfuld" means "powerful". It is built from "en magt" (power) and "fuld" (full). To say someone has strong muscles, use "stærk" (strong): "Bokseren er meget stærk" (The boxer is very strong).

sentence.da: Kongen var meget **magtfuld** og styrede hele landet.
sentence.en: The king was very powerful and ruled the whole country.

maj.explanation: "Maj" means "May". In the middle of a sentence, write the month as "maj", not "Maj": "Det er varmt i maj" (It is warm in May).

sentence.da: **Maj** kommer efter april og før juni.
sentence.en: May comes after April and before June.

majs.explanation: "Majs" means "corn", as in the vegetable. To talk about eating it, use no article: "Jeg spiser majs" (I eat corn). To point to one ear of corn, use "en majskolbe": "Jeg spiser en majskolbe" (I eat an ear of corn).

sentence.da: Popcorn er lavet af **majs**.
sentence.en: Popcorn is made of corn.

makeup.explanation: "Makeup" means "makeup". To say someone puts on makeup, use "at tage ... på" (to put on): "Hun tager makeup på" (She puts on makeup).

sentence.da: Hun bruger **makeup** på øjne og læber.
sentence.en: She uses makeup on her eyes and lips.

maksimal.explanation: "Maksimal" means "maximum". Danish spells it with "ks", not "x". For example, "maksimal". To say "at most", use "maksimalt": "Der er plads til maksimalt ti personer" (There is room for at most ten people).

sentence.da: Bilen kører med **maksimal** hastighed på motorvejen.
sentence.en: The car drives at maximum speed on the highway.

malerisk.explanation: "Malerisk" means "picturesque". It comes from "at male" (to paint). The adjective ending "-isk" also appears in "magisk" (magical) and "praktisk" (practical).

sentence.da: Den lille by med gamle huse og smalle gader er **malerisk**.
sentence.en: The small town with old houses and narrow streets is picturesque.

maling.explanation: "Maling" means "paint". To talk about a picture on a wall, use "et maleri" (a painting): "Der hænger et maleri i stuen" (A painting hangs in the living room).

sentence.da: Vi skal bruge blå **maling** til soveværelset.
sentence.en: We need blue paint for the bedroom.

man.explanation: "Man" means "you", as in anybody in general. To say something is true for anyone, use "man": "Man kan købe billetter her" (You can buy tickets here). To talk to one person, use "du" (you): "Du kan købe billetter her" (You can buy tickets here). Do not mix it up with "en mand" (a man). For example, "Der står en mand her" (A man is standing here).

sentence.da: Her må **man** ikke parkere.
sentence.en: You may not park here.

man skal ikke skue hunden på hårene.explanation: "Man skal ikke skue hunden på hårene" means "Don't judge a book by its cover". Literally, it says you should not judge the dog by its hair. The word "skue" is an old word for "look at". Use it when a person turns out different from how they looked: "Han ser sur ud." "Ja, men man skal ikke skue hunden på hårene." (He looks grumpy. Yes, but don't judge a book by its cover.)

forms.da: Man skal ikke skue hunden på hårene!
forms.en: Don't judge a book by its cover!

forms.da: Jeg troede, han var sur, men man skal ikke skue hunden på hårene
forms.en: I thought he was grumpy, but don't judge a book by its cover

related.da: det er ikke guld alt, hvad der glimrer
related.en: all that glitters is not gold

sentence.da: Hun ser streng ud, men **man skal ikke skue hunden på hårene**.
sentence.en: She looks strict, but don't judge a book by its cover.

mandag.explanation: "En mandag" means "a Monday". To say something happens on the coming Monday, use "på" (on): "Vi ses på mandag" (See you on Monday). To say it happens every Monday, say "om mandagen": "Jeg har fri om mandagen" (I am off on Mondays). To say last Monday, say "i mandags": "Vi mødtes i mandags" (We met last Monday). In the middle of a sentence, write the day as "mandag", not "Mandag".

sentence.da: Ugen begynder med **mandag**.
sentence.en: The week begins with Monday.

mandlig.explanation: "Mandlig" means "male". It is built from "en mand" (a man). To describe a male colleague, say: "en mandlig kollega" (a male colleague). To describe an animal, use the same word: "en mandlig løve" (a male lion).

sentence.da: Han er en **mandlig** sygeplejerske.
sentence.en: He is a male nurse.

manerer.explanation: "Manerer" means "manners". To say someone is well-behaved, use "at have gode manerer" (to have good manners): "Hun har gode manerer" (She has good manners).

sentence.da: Børn lærer **manerer**, når de spiser sammen med de voksne.
sentence.en: Children learn manners when they eat together with the adults.

mange.explanation: "Mange" means "many". To talk about things you can count, put it before them: "mange biler" (many cars). To talk about something you pour or measure, use "meget" (a lot, much): "meget vand" (a lot of water).

sentence.da: Jeg har **mange** venner.
sentence.en: I have many friends.

mange tak.explanation: "Mange tak" means "Thank you very much". It is a stronger thanks than "tak" (thanks). To name what you are thankful for, add "for": "Mange tak for kaffen" (Thank you very much for the coffee). To answer, say: "Mange tak!" "Selv tak." (Thank you very much! You're welcome.)

forms.en: Thank you very much for the help.

sentence.da: Her er din kaffe. – **Mange tak**!
sentence.en: Here is your coffee. – Thank you very much!

mangelfuld.explanation: "Mangelfuld" means "inadequate". It is built from "mangel" (shortage) and "-fuld" (full of), so it is literally "full of shortage". To say information is not good enough, say: "mangelfuld information" (inadequate information).

sentence.da: Forklaringen var **mangelfuld**, og vi forstod den ikke.
sentence.en: The explanation was inadequate and we did not understand it.

mangfoldighed.explanation: "Mangfoldighed" means "diversity". It is built from "mangfoldig" (diverse) and the ending "-hed". The same ending makes "frihed" (freedom) from "fri" (free).

sentence.da: Naturen byder på en stor **mangfoldighed** af planter og dyr.
sentence.en: Nature offers a great diversity of plants and animals.

manglende.explanation: "Manglende" means "missing". It comes from the verb "at mangle" (to lack). To say that a page is missing, use the verb: "Der mangler en side" (A page is missing).

sentence.da: Den **manglende** brik til puslespillet lå under sofaen.
sentence.en: The missing piece of the puzzle was under the sofa.

marcipan.explanation: "Marcipan" means "marzipan". A Danish Christmas treat is "en marcipangris" (a marzipan pig).

sentence.da: Kagen er fyldt med **marcipan** og mandler.
sentence.en: The cake is filled with marzipan and almonds.

marihuana.explanation: "Marihuana" means "marijuana". Danish spells it with an "h" where English has a "j". For example, "marihuana".

sentence.da: Det er ulovligt at sælge **marihuana** i Danmark.
sentence.en: It is illegal to sell marijuana in Denmark.

markant.explanation: "Markant" means "distinctive". To say a change is large and easy to notice, say: "en markant forbedring" (a marked improvement). To say a person stands out, say: "en markant politiker" (a prominent politician).

sentence.da: Der er en **markant** forskel mellem sommer og vinter her.
sentence.en: There is a marked difference between summer and winter here.

marmelade.explanation: "Marmelade" means "jam". Another word for jam is "syltetøj". For example, "Jeg vil have syltetøj på brødet" (I want jam on the bread).

sentence.da: Hun spiser brød med smør og **marmelade**.
sentence.en: She eats bread with butter and jam.

marmor.explanation: "Et marmor" means "marble". The word "marmor" also starts "en marmorkage" (a marble cake).

sentence.da: Statuen er hugget i **marmor**, ikke i træ.
sentence.en: The statue is carved in marble, not in wood.

marts.explanation: "Marts" means "March". To say today's date, write the month as "marts", not "Marts": "I dag er det den tiende marts" (Today is the tenth of March).

sentence.da: Efter februar kommer **marts**.
sentence.en: After February comes March.

masser af.explanation: "Masser af" means "lots of". It is literally "masses of". To say there is a large amount of something, put it before the thing: "masser af mad" (lots of food).

sentence.da: Vi har **masser af** tid i dag.
sentence.en: We have lots of time today.

matematik.explanation: "Matematik" means "math". To use the short form for the school subject, say "matte": "Jeg har matte i dag" (I have math today).

sentence.da: I **matematik** lærer vi at regne med tal.
sentence.en: In math we learn to calculate with numbers.

materiel.explanation: "Materiel" means "material", as in things you can touch or own, not ideas or feelings. For example, "materielle goder" (material goods). To talk about a substance such as wood, use "et materiale" (a material): "Træ er et godt materiale" (Wood is a good material).

sentence.da: Branden gav kun **materiel** skade, og ingen blev såret.
sentence.en: The fire caused only material damage, and nobody was hurt.

mayonnaise.explanation: "Mayonnaise" means "mayonnaise". To shorten it, say "mayo": "Vil du have mayo på?" (Do you want mayo on it?)

sentence.da: Man laver **mayonnaise** af æg og olie.
sentence.en: You make mayonnaise from egg and oil.

med.explanation: "Med" means "with". To say you are without something, use the opposite, "uden" (without): "kaffe uden mælk" (coffee without milk). To say you will go along, put "med" after the verb: "Jeg tager med" (I will come along).

forms.en: a cup of coffee with milk

sentence.da: Jeg drikker kaffe **med** mælk.
sentence.en: I drink coffee with milk.

med andre ord.explanation: "Med andre ord" means "in other words". To say the same thing again or sum it up, put it before the result: "Bilen er gået i stykker. Med andre ord må vi tage toget" (The car broke down. In other words, we must take the train).

sentence.da: Han er syg. **Med andre ord** kommer han ikke.
sentence.en: He is sick. In other words, he is not coming.

med det samme.explanation: "Med det samme" means "right away". To say something will happen soon but not now, use "om lidt" (in a little while): "Jeg kommer om lidt" (I am coming in a little while).

sentence.da: Jeg kommer **med det samme**.
sentence.en: I'm coming right away.

med forsæt.explanation: "Med forsæt" means "on purpose". It is the formal expression used in law, as in a court: "Branden blev startet med forsæt" (The fire was started on purpose). To say you did something on purpose in daily talk, use "med vilje": "Jeg gjorde det med vilje" (I did it on purpose).

sentence.da: Retten mener, at han ødelagde bilen **med forsæt**.
sentence.en: The court believes he destroyed the car on purpose.

med hensyn til.explanation: "Med hensyn til" means "regarding". To name the topic you want to talk about, say: "Med hensyn til prisen har jeg et spørgsmål" (Regarding the price, I have a question). It is literally "with consideration to".

sentence.da: **Med hensyn til** mødet i morgen kan jeg desværre ikke komme.
sentence.en: Regarding the meeting tomorrow, I unfortunately cannot come.

medfølelse.explanation: "En medfølelse" means "compassion". It is built from "med" (with) and "en følelse" (a feeling). To say whom you feel compassion for, use "med": "Hun har medfølelse med ham" (She has compassion for him).

sentence.da: Hun viste **medfølelse** og holdt ham i hånden, da han græd.
sentence.en: She showed compassion and held his hand when he cried.

medicin.explanation: "En medicin" means "a medicine". To name what a medicine is for, add "mod" (against): "medicin mod hovedpine" (medicine for a headache).

sentence.da: Jeg er syg og tager **medicin**.
sentence.en: I am sick and take medicine.

medicinsk.explanation: "Medicinsk" means "medical". It comes from "en medicin" (a medicine). To talk about treatment from a doctor, say: "medicinsk behandling" (medical treatment).

sentence.da: Lægen mener, at smerten har en **medicinsk** årsag.
sentence.en: The doctor thinks the pain has a medical cause.

medlidenhed.explanation: "En medlidenhed" means "pity". To tell someone you do not want their pity, say: "Jeg vil ikke have din medlidenhed" (I do not want your pity).

sentence.da: Han følte **medlidenhed** med hunden, som stod alene i regnen.
sentence.en: He felt pity for the dog that stood alone in the rain.

medmindre.explanation: "Medmindre" means "unless". It is built from "med" (with) and "mindre" (less). To name the one case in which something will not happen, say: "Jeg kommer, medmindre jeg bliver syg" (I will come unless I get sick).

sentence.da: Vi tager til stranden, **medmindre** det regner.
sentence.en: We are going to the beach unless it rains.

megen.explanation: "Megen" means "much". To talk about much of something that takes "en", such as "en tid" (a time), use "megen": "megen tid" (much time). To talk about much of something that takes "et", such as "et brød" (a bread), use "meget" (much): "meget brød" (much bread). To say too much, add "for" (too): "for megen støj" (too much noise).

sentence.da: Jeg har ikke **megen** tid.
sentence.en: I do not have much time.

meget.explanation: "Meget" means "very". To say very before a describing word, put "meget" in front: "meget god" (very good). To say a lot of something you cannot count, use "meget": "meget vand" (a lot of water). For things you count one by one, use "mange" (many): "mange biler" (many cars).

forms.en: I have a lot of time.

sentence.da: Det er **meget** koldt i dag.
sentence.en: It is very cold today.

mel.explanation: "Mel" means "flour". To name the grain the flour is made from, put it in front: "majsmel" (cornmeal).

sentence.da: Jeg bager brød med **mel**.
sentence.en: I bake bread with flour.

mellem.explanation: "Mellem" means "between". To name a difference, say: "forskellen mellem dem" (the difference between them). The word "mellem" also starts "et mellemrum" (a space between things).

forms.en: between the house and the forest

sentence.da: Banken ligger **mellem** posthuset og skolen.
sentence.en: The bank is between the post office and the school.

mellemøsten.explanation: "Mellemøsten" means "the Middle East". It is built from "mellem" (between) and "øst" (east). The word "mellem" also starts "et mellemmåltid" (a snack between meals).

forms.en: to travel to the Middle East
the war in the Middle East

sentence.da: Det er varmt og tørt i **Mellemøsten**.
sentence.en: It is hot and dry in the Middle East.

men.explanation: "Men" means "but". To join two ideas that go against each other, say: "Jeg er træt, men jeg kommer" (I am tired, but I am coming). To say two things happen at the same time, use "mens" (while): "Hun synger, mens hun laver mad" (She sings while she cooks).

sentence.da: Jeg er træt, **men** glad.
sentence.en: I am tired, but happy.

meningsfuld.explanation: "Meningsfuld" means "meaningful". It is built from "en mening" (a meaning) and "-fuld" (full of). The same ending is in "smertefuld" (painful).

sentence.da: Samtalen var **meningsfuld**, fordi vi endelig forstod hinanden.
sentence.en: The conversation was meaningful because we finally understood each other.

meningsløs.explanation: "Meningsløs" means "meaningless". It is built from "en mening" (a meaning) and "-løs" (without). The same ending makes "hjælpeløs" (helpless) from "hjælp" (help).

sentence.da: Diskussionen var **meningsløs**, fordi ingen ville lytte.
sentence.en: The discussion was pointless because nobody wanted to listen.

menneskehed.explanation: "Menneskehed" means "humanity". It is built from "et menneske" (a human being) and the ending "-hed". To talk about the kindness of a person, use "menneskelighed" (humaneness): "Hun viste stor menneskelighed" (She showed great humaneness).

sentence.da: Mange drømmer om en **menneskehed** uden krig.
sentence.en: Many dream of a humanity without war.

menneskelig.explanation: "Menneskelig" means "human". It is built from "et menneske" (a human being) and the ending "-lig". To say a boss is kind and understanding, say: "en menneskelig chef" (a kind boss).

sentence.da: Det er en **menneskelig** fejl, ikke en computerfejl.
sentence.en: It is a human mistake, not a computer error.

menneskerettigheder.explanation: "Menneskerettigheder" means "human rights". It is built from "et menneske" (a human being) and "en rettighed" (a right). To say a government breaks them, use "at krænke" (to violate): "Regimet krænker menneskerettighederne" (The regime violates human rights).

sentence.da: **Menneskerettigheder** gælder for alle, uanset hvor man bor.
sentence.en: Human rights apply to everyone, no matter where one lives.

mens.explanation: "Mens" means "while". To join two things that happen at the same time, say: "Hun synger, mens hun laver mad" (She sings while she cooks). To join two ideas that go against each other, use "men" (but): "Jeg er træt, men jeg kommer" (I am tired, but I am coming).

sentence.da: Jeg læser, **mens** du sover.
sentence.en: I read while you sleep.

mental sundhed.explanation: "Mental sundhed" means "mental health". The word "sundhed" comes from "sund" (healthy). To say you look after your mental health, say: "Jeg passer på min mentale sundhed" (I look after my mental health). Note that "mental" gets an "-e" there.

sentence.da: God **mental sundhed** handler om søvn, venner og ro i hverdagen.
sentence.en: Good mental health is about sleep, friends and calm in everyday life.

mentalt.explanation: "Mentalt" means "mentally". It is built from "mental" (mental) and the ending "-t". To say you are tired in your mind, say: "Jeg er mentalt træt" (I am mentally tired).

sentence.da: Før løbet forbereder løberne sig både fysisk og **mentalt**.
sentence.en: Before the race the runners prepare both physically and mentally.

mere.explanation: "Mere" means "more". To ask for more of something you cannot count, say: "mere vand" (more water). To compare a describing word, put "mere" before it: "mere interessant" (more interesting). To say something stopped, use "ikke ... mere" (not ... any longer): "Jeg bor ikke her mere" (I do not live here anymore). For things you count one by one, use "flere" (more): "flere biler" (more cars).

sentence.da: Jeg er sulten og vil have **mere** mad.
sentence.en: I am hungry and want more food.

mest.explanation: "Mest" means "most". To say you mostly do something, put "mest" before the thing: "Jeg læser mest krimier" (I mostly read crime novels). To say a describing word is at the top, put "mest" before it: "mest interessant" (most interesting).

sentence.da: Jeg kan **mest** lide kaffe.
sentence.en: I like coffee the most.

mexicansk.explanation: "Mexicansk" means "Mexican". To talk about a person from Mexico, use "en mexicaner" (a Mexican person): "Han er mexicaner" (He is Mexican).

sentence.da: Vi spiser **mexicansk** mad hver fredag.
sentence.en: We eat Mexican food every Friday.

middelalderen.explanation: "Middelalderen" means "the Middle Ages". It is built from "middel" (middle) and "en alder" (an age). To describe something from that time, put "middelalder" in front of a noun: "en middelalderby" (a medieval town).

sentence.da: I **middelalderen** boede de fleste danskere på landet og dyrkede jorden.
sentence.en: In the Middle Ages most Danes lived in the countryside and farmed the land.

midlertidig.explanation: "Midlertidig" means "temporary". To say something is closed for a short time, use "midlertidigt": "Butikken er midlertidigt lukket" (The shop is temporarily closed).

sentence.da: Broen er **midlertidig**, fordi den nye bro ikke er færdig.
sentence.en: The bridge is temporary because the new bridge is not finished.

midnat.explanation: "Midnat" means "midnight". Do not mix it up with "middag" (dinner). To say what time you eat dinner, use it for the meal: "Vi spiser middag klokken seks" (We eat dinner at six).

sentence.da: Festen slutter først ved **midnat**.
sentence.en: The party only ends at midnight.

midt.explanation: "Midt" means "in the middle". To say where the middle of a place is, use "midt i" (in the middle of): "midt i byen" (in the middle of town). To say the middle of a part of the day, use "midt på" (in the middle of): "midt på dagen" (in the middle of the day).

forms.en: in the middle of the room
in the middle of the night

sentence.da: Der står et træ **midt** i haven.
sentence.en: There is a tree in the middle of the garden.

mig.explanation: "Mig" means "me". When you are the one doing the action, use "jeg" (I) instead: "Jeg ser ham" (I see him). When you do something to yourself, "mig" means "myself": "Jeg vasker mig" (I wash myself). After "til" (to) and "med" (with), use "mig" too: "til mig" (to me), "med mig" (with me).

sentence.da: Min ven giver **mig** en gave.
sentence.en: My friend gives me a gift.

mild.explanation: "Mild" means "mild". To talk about the weather, use it for a season: "Vinteren er mild i år" (The winter is mild this year). To talk about food that is not strong, use it for a food: "en mild ost" (a mild cheese).

sentence.da: Jeg vil have en **mild** sauce uden chili.
sentence.en: I want a mild sauce without chili.

militær.explanation: "Militær" means "military". When you talk about the whole armed forces, add "-et" to make the noun: "militæret" (the military). To say someone serves in them: "Han er i militæret" (He is in the military).

sentence.da: Soldaterne træner på en **militær** base uden for byen.
sentence.en: The soldiers train at a military base outside the town.

million.explanation: "En million" means "a million". English never adds an ending to "million" after a number, but Danish does. To say two million, use: "to millioner mennesker" (two million people). Do not mix it up with "en milliard" (a billion, which is 1,000 million). To say how much money, use: "en milliard kroner" (a billion kroner).

sentence.da: Han vandt en **million** kroner i lotteriet.
sentence.en: He won a million kroner in the lottery.

min.explanation: "Min" means "my". To say my car, use it with one car: "min bil" (my car). With one house, use "mit" instead: "mit hus" (my house). With more than one thing, use "mine": "mine børn" (my children).

related.en: your (with one thing like a car)

sentence.da: Jeg har en bil. **Min** bil er rød.
sentence.en: I have a car. My car is red.

mindre.explanation: "Mindre" means "less". When you describe the size of a thing, it means "smaller": "et mindre hus" (a smaller house). Do not mix it up with "mindst" (least). For example, "Hun har mindst penge" (She has the least money).

sentence.da: Et lille hus er **mindre** end et stort.
sentence.en: A small house is smaller than a big one.

mindst.explanation: "Mindst" means "least". To ask who has the smallest amount of something, use it before the thing: "Hvem har mindst tid?" (Who has the least time?) To give the lowest number that is fine, use it before a number, where it means "at least": "mindst fem" (at least five).

forms.en: I will wait at least an hour

sentence.da: Du skal sove **mindst** otte timer.
sentence.en: You should sleep at least eight hours.

mine.explanation: "Mine" means "my". When you talk about more than one thing, use it: "mine huse" (my houses). With one house, use "mit" instead: "mit hus" (my house). With one book, use "min" instead: "min bog" (my book).

sentence.da: **Mine** børn hedder Peter og Anna.
sentence.en: My children are called Peter and Anna.

minigolf.explanation: "Minigolf" means "mini golf". Unlike the English spelling, Danish has no space inside "minigolf".

sentence.da: I **minigolf** slår man bolden gennem en lille tunnel.
sentence.en: In mini golf, you hit the ball through a small tunnel.

minimal.explanation: "Minimal" means "minimal". Its opposite is "maksimal" (maximum). To say the highest speed that is possible, use the opposite: "maksimal hastighed" (maximum speed).

sentence.da: Risikoen for fejl er **minimal**, fordi alt bliver tjekket to gange.
sentence.en: The risk of errors is minimal because everything is checked twice.

misfornøjet.explanation: "Misfornøjet" means "dissatisfied". It is built from "mis-" and "fornøjet" (pleased). The start "mis-" also works like English "mis-" in "at misforstå" (to misunderstand).

sentence.da: Kunden var **misfornøjet**, fordi maden kom for sent.
sentence.en: The customer was dissatisfied because the food came too late.

misforstået.explanation: "Misforstået" means "misunderstood". It comes from the verb "at misforstå" (to misunderstand). To call a feeling or loyalty misguided, use it too: "misforstået loyalitet" (misguided loyalty).

sentence.da: Hendes joke blev **misforstået**, så hun forklarede den igen.
sentence.en: Her joke was misunderstood, so she explained it again.

misinformation.explanation: "Misinformation" means "misinformation". Do not mix it up with "desinformation" (disinformation). Misinformation is false information spread by mistake. For example, "Det er misinformation" (That is misinformation). Disinformation is false information spread on purpose. For another example, "Det er desinformation" (That is disinformation).

sentence.da: **Misinformation** spredes hurtigt på sociale medier, selv når folk mener det godt.
sentence.en: Misinformation spreads quickly on social media, even when people mean well.

mistillid.explanation: "En mistillid" means "distrust". It is built from "mis-" and "tillid" (trust). To talk about a vote of no confidence in a government, use "et mistillidsvotum": "Der er et mistillidsvotum mod regeringen" (There is a vote of no confidence against the government).

sentence.da: Der er stor **mistillid** mellem de to lande efter krigen.
sentence.en: There is great distrust between the two countries after the war.

mistænkelig.explanation: "Mistænkelig" means "suspicious". Do not mix it up with "mistænksom" (suspicious of others). To say a thing seems wrong, use "mistænkelig": "en mistænkelig lyd" (a suspicious sound). To say a person does not trust others, use "mistænksom": "en mistænksom nabo" (a neighbor who distrusts others).

sentence.da: Manden virkede **mistænkelig**, fordi han skjulte sit ansigt.
sentence.en: The man seemed suspicious because he hid his face.

mistænksom.explanation: "Mistænksom" means "suspicious". Do not mix it up with "mistænkelig" (looking suspicious). To say a person does not trust others, use "mistænksom": "en mistænksom nabo" (a neighbor who distrusts others). To say a thing seems wrong, use "mistænkelig": "en mistænkelig lyd" (a suspicious sound).

sentence.da: Hunden er **mistænksom** over for fremmede, og den gøer højt.
sentence.en: The dog is suspicious of strangers, and it barks loudly.

mistænkt.explanation: "Mistænkt" means "suspected". To name the person the police are looking at, use the noun "en mistænkt" (a suspect): "Politiet har en mistænkt" (The police have a suspect).

sentence.da: Manden er **mistænkt** for tyveriet, men han nægter.
sentence.en: The man is suspected of the theft, but he denies it.

misundelig.explanation: "Misundelig" means "envious". To say who you envy, add "på" (of): "Han er misundelig på sin kollega" (He is envious of his coworker).

sentence.da: Jeg er **misundelig** på din nye bil.
sentence.en: I am envious of your new car.

misundelse.explanation: "En misundelse" means "envy". Do not mix it up with "jalousi" (jealousy), the fear of losing a partner to someone else. To talk about that fear, say: "Jalousi kan ødelægge et forhold" (Jealousy can ruin a relationship).

sentence.da: Hun følte **misundelse**, da veninden fik et drømmejob.
sentence.en: She felt envy when her friend got a dream job.

misvisende.explanation: "Misvisende" means "misleading". The start "mis-" also appears in "at misforstå" (to misunderstand) and "mistillid" (distrust).

sentence.da: Overskriften er **misvisende**, fordi artiklen siger noget andet.
sentence.en: The headline is misleading because the article says something else.

mit.explanation: "Mit" means "my". Use it with one thing that takes "et", as in "mit værelse" (my room). With one car, use "min" instead: "min bil" (my car). With more than one thing, use "mine": "mine børn" (my children).

related.en: your (with one thing like a room)

sentence.da: Jeg har et hus. **Mit** hus er gult.
sentence.en: I have a house. My house is yellow.

mod.explanation: "Mod" means "toward". To point to a direction, use it before the place: "Han går mod døren" (He walks toward the door). When you play an opponent, it means "against": "Danmark spiller mod Norge" (Denmark plays against Norway). To say you are against an idea, use "imod" (against) instead: "Jeg er imod det" (I am against it).

sentence.da: Vi går **mod** stationen.
sentence.en: We are walking toward the station.

mode.explanation: "Mode" means "fashion". Do not mix it up with "en måde" (a way). To say a good way to learn, say: "Det er en god måde at lære på" (That is a good way to learn).

sentence.da: Min søster elsker **mode** og køber meget tøj.
sentence.en: My sister loves fashion and buys a lot of clothes.

moderigtig.explanation: "Moderigtig" means "fashionable". It is built from "mode" (fashion) and "rigtig" (right), so it is literally "right for the fashion".

sentence.da: Jakken er **moderigtig** nu, men måske ikke næste år.
sentence.en: The jacket is fashionable now, but maybe not next year.

moderne.explanation: "Moderne" means "modern". To say something is not modern, use the opposite, "gammeldags" (old-fashioned): "et gammeldags køkken" (an old-fashioned kitchen).

sentence.da: Vi bor i et **moderne** hus med store vinduer.
sentence.en: We live in a modern house with big windows.

modgang.explanation: "En modgang" means "adversity". Its opposite is "medgang" (good fortune). To say through good times and bad, use both words together: "i medgang og modgang" (in good times and bad).

sentence.da: Gode venner står ved din side, når du har **modgang**.
sentence.en: Good friends stand by your side when you face adversity.

modig.explanation: "Modig" means "brave". It comes from "mod" (courage). To say you are scared instead, use "bange" (scared): "Jeg er bange for edderkopper" (I am scared of spiders).

sentence.da: Hun er **modig** og tør tale foran hundrede mennesker.
sentence.en: She is brave and dares to speak in front of a hundred people.

modløs.explanation: "Modløs" means "discouraged". It is built from "mod" (courage) and "-løs" (without), so it is literally "without courage".

sentence.da: Efter det dårlige resultat blev hun **modløs** og ville give op.
sentence.en: After the bad result she became discouraged and wanted to give up.

modsat.explanation: "Modsat" means "opposite". To name the opposite thing itself, say "det modsatte": "Det modsatte af varm er kold" (The opposite of hot is cold).

sentence.da: Han gik til højre, og jeg gik i **modsat** retning.
sentence.en: He went right, and I went in the opposite direction.

modstandsdygtig.explanation: "Modstandsdygtig" means "resilient". It is built from "modstand" (resistance) and "dygtig" (skilled).

sentence.da: Planten er **modstandsdygtig** og klarer sig godt i frost.
sentence.en: The plant is resilient and does well in frost.

moms.explanation: "Moms" means "VAT". To ask whether the price includes VAT, say: "Er det med moms?" (Is VAT included?)

sentence.da: Prisen er tusind kroner med **moms**.
sentence.en: The price is a thousand kroner with VAT.

moralsk.explanation: "Moralsk" means "moral". To say you are bound by what is right, use it with "pligt" (duty): "en moralsk pligt" (a moral duty).

sentence.da: Er det forkert at lyve? Det er et **moralsk** spørgsmål.
sentence.en: Is it wrong to lie? That is a moral question.

morgenmad.explanation: "Morgenmad" means "breakfast". It is built from "morgen" (morning) and "mad" (food). When you mean breakfast in general, leave out "en": "Jeg spiser morgenmad" (I eat breakfast).

sentence.da: Om morgenen spiser jeg **morgenmad**: brød og kaffe.
sentence.en: In the morning I eat breakfast: bread and coffee.

morsom.explanation: "Morsom" means "amusing". To say a story makes you smile, use it: "en morsom historie" (an amusing story). Do not mix it up with "sjov" (fun, funny). For example, "Festen var sjov" (The party was fun).

sentence.da: Han er **morsom** og får alle til at le.
sentence.en: He is funny and makes everyone laugh.

mos.explanation: "Et mos" means "moss or mash". To talk about the green plant on a roof, say: "Der er mos på taget" (There is moss on the roof). To talk about mashed potatoes, put "kartoffel" (potato) in front: "Jeg laver kartoffelmos" (I am making mashed potatoes).

sentence.da: Der vokser **mos** på de gamle sten.
sentence.en: Moss grows on the old stones.

motion.explanation: "Motion" means "exercise", as in physical activity. For an exercise in a lesson, use "en øvelse" (an exercise): "en øvelse i grammatik" (a grammar exercise).

sentence.da: Jeg går en lang tur for at få **motion**.
sentence.en: I take a long walk to get exercise.

motivation.explanation: "Motivation" means "motivation". It is the noun for the verb "at motivere" (to motivate).

sentence.da: Jeg har ingen **motivation** til at træne.
sentence.en: I have no motivation to exercise.

mozzarella.explanation: "Mozzarella" means "mozzarella". To say what a pizza has on it, use "med" (with): "pizza med mozzarella" (pizza with mozzarella).

sentence.da: Til salaten køber jeg frisk **mozzarella** og tomater.
sentence.en: For the salad, I buy fresh mozzarella and tomatoes.

mudder.explanation: "Et mudder" means "mud". To say you are stuck in it, use "fast i" (stuck in): "Bilen sidder fast i mudderet" (The car is stuck in the mud).

sentence.da: Efter regnen var marken fuld af **mudder**.
sentence.en: After the rain the field was full of mud.

mulig.explanation: "Mulig" means "possible". To ask someone to hurry, use the set phrase "så hurtigt som muligt" (as fast as possible): "Kom så hurtigt som muligt" (Come as fast as possible).

sentence.da: Regn er **mulig** i morgen, men ikke sikker.
sentence.en: Rain is possible tomorrow, but not certain.

muligvis.explanation: "Muligvis" means "possibly". It is built from "mulig" (possible). To answer a question with one word, say: "Kommer hun?" "Muligvis." (Is she coming? Possibly.)

sentence.da: Vi tager **muligvis** til Spanien i sommer.
sentence.en: We are possibly going to Spain this summer.

mundtlig.explanation: "Mundtlig" means "oral". It comes from "en mund" (a mouth), so it is literally "of the mouth". To say an exam is done in writing, use the opposite, "skriftlig" (written): "en skriftlig eksamen" (a written exam).

sentence.da: Jeg skal ikke skrive, fordi eksamen er **mundtlig**.
sentence.en: I do not have to write because the exam is oral.

munter.explanation: "Munter" means "cheerful". To describe a tune that sounds happy, use it too: "en munter melodi" (a cheerful tune).

sentence.da: Hun var **munter** og sang hele vejen hjem.
sentence.en: She was cheerful and sang all the way home.

musik.explanation: "Musik" means "music". This word has no article when it means music in general, so leave out "en". For example, "Jeg elsker musik" (I love music). To say a school lesson is music, use "at have" (to have): "Vi har musik i dag" (We have music today).

sentence.da: Jeg lytter gerne til **musik**.
sentence.en: I like listening to music.

musikalsk.explanation: "Musikalsk" means "musical". It comes from the noun "musik" (music). To describe a whole family, use it too: "en musikalsk familie" (a musical family).

sentence.da: Min datter er meget **musikalsk** og elsker at synge.
sentence.en: My daughter is very musical and loves to sing.

muskuløs.explanation: "Muskuløs" means "muscular". It comes from "en muskel" (a muscle). Do not mix it up with "stærk" (strong). To say a man has power but not big muscles, say: "Han er stærk, men ikke muskuløs" (He is strong, but not muscular).

sentence.da: Gymnasten er **muskuløs**, fordi han træner hver dag.
sentence.en: The gymnast is muscular because he trains every day.

muslimsk.explanation: "Muslimsk" means "Muslim". To name a person, use the noun "en muslim" (a Muslim): "Min nabo er muslim" (My neighbor is a Muslim). To describe a custom or a prayer, use "muslimsk": "en muslimsk bøn" (a Muslim prayer).

sentence.da: Ramadanen er en **muslimsk** tradition.
sentence.en: Ramadan is a Muslim tradition.

mystisk.explanation: "Mystisk" means "mysterious". To describe a sound at night that you cannot explain, use it: "en mystisk lyd om natten" (a mysterious sound at night). Do not mix it up with "mærkelig" (strange). To describe something that is only odd, use "mærkelig": "en mærkelig hat" (a strange hat).

sentence.da: Der står en **mystisk** mand uden for vores dør.
sentence.en: A mysterious man is standing outside our door.

mytologi.explanation: "En mytologi" means "a mythology". To name the old stories of one people, put the people before it: "den græske mytologi" (Greek mythology).

sentence.da: Thor er en figur i den nordiske **mytologi**.
sentence.en: Thor is a figure in Norse mythology.

må jeg bede om regningen?.explanation: "Må jeg bede om regningen?" means "May I have the bill?". Literally, "bede om" means "ask for", so it asks "May I ask for the bill?". To ask for something else, keep the start and change the end: "Må jeg bede om et glas vand?" (May I have a glass of water?)

sentence.da: Vi har spist. **Må jeg bede om regningen?**
sentence.en: We have eaten. May I have the bill?

må jeg få regningen?.explanation: "Må jeg få regningen?" means "May I have the bill?". Literally, "få" means "get", so it asks "May I get the bill?". To ask for something else, keep the start and change the end: "Må jeg få et glas vand?" (May I have a glass of water?)

forms.da: Må jeg få en kop kaffe?
forms.en: May I have a cup of coffee?

sentence.da: Maden var god. **Må jeg få regningen?**
sentence.en: The food was good. May I have the bill?

målrettet.explanation: "Målrettet" means "goal-oriented". It is built from "et mål" (a goal) and "rettet" (aimed).

sentence.da: Hun er **målrettet** og ved præcis, hvad hun vil.
sentence.en: She is goal-oriented and knows exactly what she wants.

månedsvis.explanation: "Månedsvis" means "months", as in lasting for months. It is built from "en måned" (a month) and the ending "-vis". To say how long you waited, put it after the verb: "Vi har ventet månedsvis" (We have waited for months).

sentence.da: Vi ventede **månedsvis** på svar fra kommunen.
sentence.en: We waited for months for an answer from the municipality.

måske.explanation: "Måske" means "maybe". To answer a question when you are not sure, say: "Kommer du?" "Måske." (Are you coming? Maybe.)

sentence.da: **Måske** kommer han i morgen.
sentence.en: Maybe he will come tomorrow.

mægtig.explanation: "Mægtig" means "mighty". It comes from "en magt" (a power). To say a tree is huge and impressive, use it: "et mægtigt træ" (a mighty tree).

sentence.da: Ørnen er en **mægtig** fugl med store vinger.
sentence.en: The eagle is a mighty bird with large wings.

mælk.explanation: "Mælk" means "milk". To say how much milk, use a measure first: "en liter mælk" (a liter of milk).

sentence.da: Jeg drikker et glas **mælk** hver morgen.
sentence.en: I drink a glass of milk every morning.

mærkbar.explanation: "Mærkbar" means "noticeable". It is built from "at mærke" (to feel) and "-bar" (able to be). Do not mix it up with "mærkelig" (strange). For example, "en mærkelig lyd" (a strange sound).

sentence.da: Forskellen er **mærkbar**, og alle kan se den.
sentence.en: The difference is noticeable and everyone can see it.

mærkelig.explanation: "Mærkelig" means "strange". It comes from "at mærke" (to notice). Do not mix it up with "mærkbar" (noticeable). For example, "en mærkbar forskel" (a noticeable difference).

sentence.da: Der er en **mærkelig** lyd i køkkenet.
sentence.en: There is a strange sound in the kitchen.

mæt.explanation: "Mæt" means "full", as in having eaten enough. To say you have eaten enough, say: "Jeg er mæt" (I am full). After a meal, do not say "Jeg er fuld", because "fuld" means "drunk".

sentence.da: Jeg har spist meget og er **mæt**.
sentence.en: I have eaten a lot and am full.

mættende.explanation: "Mættende" means "filling". It comes from the verb "at mætte" (to fill up). Do not mix it up with "mæt" (full), which describes a person. For example, "Jeg er mæt" (I am full). "Mættende" describes food. For another example, "en mættende suppe" (a filling soup).

sentence.da: Havregrød er **mættende**, og man bliver ikke hurtigt sulten.
sentence.en: Oatmeal is filling and you do not get hungry quickly.

møbleret.explanation: "Møbleret" means "furnished". It comes from the verb "at møblere" (to furnish). To say a place has no furniture, add "u-": "en umøbleret lejlighed" (an unfurnished apartment).

sentence.da: Værelset er **møbleret** med seng, bord og stol.
sentence.en: The room is furnished with a bed, table and chair.

mør.explanation: "Mør" means "tender". To say meat is hard to chew, use the opposite, "sej" (tough): "Kødet er sejt" (The meat is tough). In "en mørbrad" (a tenderloin), the part "mør" means "tender".

sentence.da: Kødet er **mør**, fordi det har stået længe i ovnen.
sentence.en: The meat is tender because it has been in the oven a long time.

mørk.explanation: "Mørk" means "dark". In color names, the form "mørke-" (dark) goes first. For example, "mørkeblå" (dark blue).

sentence.da: Om natten er himlen **mørk**.
sentence.en: At night the sky is dark.

mørke.explanation: "Mørke" means "darkness". Do not mix it up with "mørk" (dark). To describe a room without light, use "mørk": "et mørkt rum" (a dark room).

sentence.da: Vi sidder i **mørke**, når strømmen går.
sentence.en: We sit in the dark when the power goes out.

mørkeblå.explanation: "Mørkeblå" means "dark blue". It is built from "mørk" (dark) and "blå" (blue). To say a blue is bright like a clear sky, use "himmelblå" (sky blue): "en himmelblå trøje" (a sky-blue sweater).

sentence.da: Himlen er **mørkeblå** før solopgang.
sentence.en: The sky is dark blue before sunrise.

mørkegrøn.explanation: "Mørkegrøn" means "dark green". It is built from "mørk" (dark) and "grøn" (green). To say a green is fresh like grass, use "græsgrøn" (grass green): "en græsgrøn plæne" (a grass-green lawn).

sentence.da: Granen er **mørkegrøn** hele året.
sentence.en: The fir tree is dark green all year.

mørketid.explanation: "En mørketid" means "a dark season". It is built from "mørke" (darkness) and "tid" (time).

sentence.da: I årets **mørketid** er dagene meget korte.
sentence.en: In the dark season of the year the days are very short.

mørkhåret.explanation: "Mørkhåret" means "dark-haired". It is built from "mørk" (dark), "hår" (hair) and the ending "-et". To say someone has blue eyes, the same pattern works: "en blåøjet pige" (a blue-eyed girl).

sentence.da: Han er høj og **mørkhåret**, og han har blå øjne.
sentence.en: He is tall and dark-haired, and he has blue eyes.

müsli.explanation: "Müsli" means "muesli". Danish spells it with "ü" and no "e", unlike the English spelling.

sentence.da: Jeg spiser **müsli** med mælk i en skål.
sentence.en: I eat muesli with milk in a bowl.
